        1. 3.3.1.1 JEALOUSY.

        1. 3.3.2.1 Symptoms of Jealousy, fear, sorrow, suspicion, strange actions, gestures, outrages, locking up, oaths, trials, laws, &c.

        1. 3.3.3.1 Prognostics of Jealousy, Despair, Madness, to make away themselves and others.

        1. 3.3.4.1 Cure of Jealousy: by avoiding occasions, not to be idle: of good counsel: to contemn it, not to watch or lock them up: to dissemble it, &c.

      1. Member 1
        1. 3.4.1.1 Religious Melancholy.
        2. 3.4.1.2 Causes of Religious melancholy. From the Devil by miracles, apparitions, oracles. His instruments or factors, politicians, Priests, Impostors, Heretics, blind guides. In them simplicity, fear, blind zeal, ignorance, solitariness, curiosity, pride, vainglory, presumption, &c. His engines, fasting, solitariness, hope, fear, &c.
        3. 3.4.1.3 Symptoms general, love to their own sect, hate of all other Religions, obstinacy, peevishness, ready to undergo any danger or cross for it; Martyrs, blind zeal, blind obedience, fastings, vows, belief of incredibilities, impossibilities: Particular of Gentiles, Mahometans, Jews, Christians; and in them, Heretics old and new, Schismatics, Schoolmen, Prophets, Enthusiasts, &c.
        4. 3.4.1.4 Prognostics of Religious Melancholy.
        5. 3.4.1.5 Cure of Religious Melancholy.

        1. 3.4.2.1 Religious Melancholy in defect; parties affected, Epicures, Atheists, Hypocrites, worldly secure, Carnalists, all impious persons, Impenitent sinners, &c.

        3. 3.4.2.3 Causes of despair, the Devil, melancholy, meditation, Distrust, weakness of faith, rigid Ministers, misunderstanding Scriptures, guilty consciences, &c.
        4. 3.4.2.4 Symptoms of Despair, Fear, Sorrow, Suspicion, Anxiety, Horror of conscience, fearful dreams and visions.
        5. 3.4.2.5 Prognostics of Despair, Atheism, Blasphemy, violent death, &c.
        6. 3.4.2.6 Cure of Despair by Physic, good counsel, comforts, &c.

They are commonly slaves, captives, voluntary servants, ⁂Ama­tor ami­cae man­ci­piumTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Burton translates: “his Mistress’ servant, her drudge, prisoner, bondman”Burton’s own renderingthe lover, slave of his girlfriendg [the lover, slave of his girlfriend], as jj cites Lib. 3 de aulico.Baldassare Castiglione, Il Cortegiano (De aulico), book 3 .Castilio terms him, his Mistress’ servant, her drudge, prisoner, bondman, what not? He composeth himself wholly to her affections, to please her; and as Emilia said, makes himself her lackey. All his cares, actions, all his thoughts, are subordinate to her will and commandment; her most devote, obsequious, affectionate servant and vassal. For love (as kk cites Cyroped. lib. 5.Xenophon, Cyropaedia, book 5 .Cyrus in Xenophon well observed) is a mere tyranny, worse than any disease, and they that are troubled with it, desire to be free and cannot, but are harder bound than if they were in iron chains. What greater captivity or slavery can there be (as ll note In paradoxis.Tully expostulates) than to be in love? Is he a free man over whom a woman domineers, to whom she prescribes Laws, commands, forbids what she will herself? That dares deny nothing she demands; she asks, he gives; she calls, he comes; she threatens, he fears; ⁂ne­quis­si­mum hunc ser­vum putoTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.Burton translates: “I account this man a very drudge”Burton’s own rendering I reckon this man the most worthless of slaves , I account this man a very drudge. And as he follows it, °° note Illane parva est servitus amatorum singulis fere horis pectine capillum, calimistroque barbam componere, faciem aquis redolentibus diluere, &c. dmAuthor trans. “Is this no small servitude for an enamorate to be every hour combing his head, stiffening his beard, perfuming his hair, washing his face with sweet waters” Is this no small servitude for an enamorate to be every hour combing his head, stiffening his beard, perfuming his hair, washing his face with sweet waters, painting, curling, and not to come abroad but sprucely crowned, decked and apparelled? Yet these are but toys in respect to go to the Barber, Baths, Theatres, &c., he must attend upon her wherever she goes, run along the streets by her doors and windows to see her, take all opportunities, sleeveless errands, disguise, counterfeit shapes, and as many forms as Jupiter himself ever took; and come every day to her house (as he will surely do if he be truly enamoured) and offer her service, and follow her up and down from room to room, as Lucretia’s suitors did, he cannot contain himself but he will do it, he must and will be where she is, sit next her, still talking with her. °° note Si quando in pavimentum incautius quid mihi excidisset, elevare inde quam promptissime, nec nisi osculo compacto mihi commendare, &c. dmAuthor trans. “If I did but let my glove fall by chance (as the said Aretine’s Lucretia brags), I had one of my suitors, nay two or three at once ready to stoop and take it up, and kiss it, and with a long congee deliver it unto me” If I did but let my glove fall by chance (as the said Aretine’s Lucretia brags), I had one of my suitors, nay two or three at once ready to stoop and take it up, and kiss it, and with a long congee deliver it unto me: if I would walk, another was ready to sustain me by the arm. A third to provide fruits, Pears, Plums, Cherries, or whatsoever I would eat or drink. All this and much more he doth in her presence, and when he comes home, as Troilus on his Criseyde, ’tis all his meditation to recount with himself her actions, words, gestures, what entertainment he had, how kindly she used him in such a place, how she smiled, how she graced him, and that infinitely pleased him; then he breaks out, O sweet Areusa, O my dearest Antiphila, O most divine looks, O lovely graces, and thereupon instantly he makes an Epigram, or a Sonnet to five or seven tunes, in her commendation, or else he ruminates how she rejected his service, denied him a kiss, disgraced him, &c., and that as effectually torments him. And these are his exercises betwixt comb and glass, Madrigals, Elegies, &c., these his cogitations till he see her again. But all this is easy and gentle, and the least part of his labour and bondage, no hunter will take such pains for his Game, Fowler for his sport, or Soldier to sack a City, as he will for his Mistress’ favour.

for her sweet sake he will undertake Hercules’ twelve labours, endure hazard, &c., he feels it not. nn cites Lib. 1 de contem. amor.Pietro Edo (Petrus Haedus), De contemnendis amoribus, book 1 .What shall I say (saith Haedus) of their great dangers they undergo, single combats they undertake, how they will venture their lives, creep in at windows, gutters, climb over walls to come to their sweethearts (anointing the doors and hinges with oil, because they should not creak, tread soft, swim, wade, watch, &c.), and if they be surprised, leap out at windows, cast themselves headlong down, bruising or breaking their legs or arms, and sometimes losing life itself, as Calisto did for his lovely Melibea. Boccace hath a pleasant tale to this purpose, which he borrowed from the Greeks, and which Beroaldus hath turned into Latin, Bebelius into verse, of Cymon and Iphigenia. This Cymon was a fool, a proper man of person, and the Governor of Cyprus’ son, but a very ass, insomuch that his father being ashamed of him, sent him to a Farmhouse he had in the country to be brought up. Where by chance, as his manner was, walking alone, he espied a gallant young Gentlewoman named Iphigenia, a Burgomaster’s daughter of Cyprus with her maid, by a brook-side in a little thicket, fast asleep in her smock, where she had newly bathed herself: when °° note Hanc ubi conspicatus est Cymon, baculo innixus, immobilis stetit, et mirabundus, &c. dmAuthor trans. “Cymon saw her, he stood leaning on his staff, gaping on her, immovable, and in a maze” Cymon saw her, he stood leaning on his staff, gaping on her, immovable, and in a maze: at last he fell so far in love with the glorious object, that he began to rouse himself up, to bethink what he was, would needs follow her to the city, and for her sake began to be civil, to learn to sing and dance, to play on Instruments, and got all those Gentlemen-like qualities and complements in a short space, which his friends were most glad of. In brief, he became from an Idiot and a clown, to be one of the most complete Gentlemen in Cyprus, did many valorous exploits, and all for the love of Mistress Iphigenia. With tokens, hearts divided, and half rings,Shepherds in their Loves are as coy as Kings.

Corydon’s Phyllis, Nysa and Mopsus,With dainty Dousabel and Sir Tophas.

Translation from Latin: from LatinLat.I don’t know what love is, nor do I love …gI know not what love is, nor do I love — The line breaks off at Burton's dash. Burton uses it to claim, half in jest, that he has no experience of love, and he qualifies the claim straight away in the next sentence.

In full it reads 'homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto': 'I am a man; I count nothing human foreign to me.' Here it serves as his excuse for knowing something about love.. [I’m a man, etc.], not altogether inexpert in this subject, non sum prae­cep­tor amandiTranslation from Latin: from LatinLat.I’m not an instructor in lovinggI am not a teacher of love,djI am no teacher of loving This seems to turn around Ovid's boast in the Art of Love that he was a 'praeceptor Amoris', a teacher of Love. [from others’ absurdities perhaps], by mine own observation, and others’ relation.

trans. All in love are pale: it’s the right colour for the lover g

Burton's 'plurima currit Imago' is not Virgil's wording, so the second line is rendered by its sense.
trans. My love does not subside / When the evening star is rising, / Or when it’s fleeing the onrushing sun; g
moreNor do my loves depart from me when the evening star / rises, / nor when it flees the swift sun; Source Burton cites Horace, Odes, book 2, ode 9 (unverified)
Horace has 'nec tibi' (your loves, addressed to Valgius). Burton changes it to 'mihi' to make it a lover's own complaint. trans. Awake, I seek you with my eyes; at night, with my mind. g
moreThee with waking eyes and anxious mind I follow all night. djWaking, I seek you with my eyes; at night, with my mind. Source Burton cites Petronius (unverified)
trans. The soul exists not where it gives life, but where it loves g
moreThe soul is not where it lives, but where it loves. djThe soul is not where it gives life, but where it loves. Notes Plays on animat ('gives life to') and amat ('loves'). A proverbial saying of the schools, attributed to several medieval writers. Burton's following English gives the general idea loosely; it does not translate the line.
Author trans. “a cloud for Juno”
literala cloud instead of Juno
Author trans. “I see and meditate of naught but Leucippe”
literalI see nothing but Leucippe; Leucippe is always before my eyes and turning in my mind.
trans. And although the presence of that pleasing beauty was absent, / The love, to which its presence had given form, remained. g
moreThough her fair presence is wanting. The love which it kindled stays, djAnd though the presence of her gentle beauty was gone, / the love that her beauty had given while present remained. Source Burton cites Ovid, Fasti, 2 ver. 775 (unverified)Notes Tarquin's passion for Lucretia after he has left her.
trans. and when awake he seemed to be having intercourse with her g
moreand he seemed, while awake, to lie with her Source Burton cites Ulrich Molitor, De Pythonicis (unverified)Notes Commisceri means sexual union. Burton's 'still embracing him' softens it.
trans. a torment of the mind g
moreanguish of mind
trans. every lover wages war g
moreevery lover is a soldier Source Probably Ovid, Amores, 1.9.1 (unverified)
The opening of Ovid's elegy comparing love to military service. trans. come closer to this flame, etc. g
morecome near this fire, etc. Source Burton cites Terence, Eunuchus (unverified)Notes Terence has 'accede ad ignem hunc'. Burton's 'hanc' is feminine, though ignis is masculine. In the play the line goes on: 'you will soon be more than warm enough'.
trans. … My torment feeds and grows, / And burns inside, like the steam / That flows from the crater of Etna … g
more— the evil is fed and grows, / and burns within, as the vapour / pours out from Etna's cave — Source Burton cites Seneca, Hippolytus (Phaedra) (unverified)Notes Phaedra describing her passion. Seneca's Phaedra was also known as Hippolytus.
trans. … For love often burns hotter / Than the flame of Liparian Vulcan. g
more— For love often kindles a flame / hotter than Liparean Vulcan. Source Burton cites Theocritus, Idylls, idyl. 2 (unverified)
A Latin version of Theocritus. Vulcan's forge was placed in the Lipari islands. Author trans. “’tis a fire in a fire”
literalFire rages within fire
trans. We burn, and our feelings bear the hidden wound, g
moreburn, and my breast hath a secret wound, djWe burn, and our breast holds an unseen wound, Source Burton cites Ovid (unverified)Notes caecum, literally 'blind', here means hidden or unseen. The line is probably Ovid, Heroides 4 (Phaedra to Hippolytus), but Burton gives only 'Ovid.'.
Author trans. “so doth Love dry up his radical moisture”
literalso blind love consumes its own vitals,
trans. … The interrupted works are left hanging, / The huge menacing walls, and the sky-reaching cranes. g
moreThe works unfinished hang, the threatening walls. And turrets mounting upward to the skies, dj— the works hang broken off, the huge threatening walls, / and the crane that rose level with the sky. Source Burton cites Virgil, Aeneid, 4 (unverified)
Carthage's building stops while Dido is in love. minae murorum are the towering, menacing walls; machina is a building crane or derrick. trans. … the loom of Athena stands idle, / And the wool slips between my very hands. g
moreThe web of Pallas languishes, the work Even in Phcedra's hands is left undone. dj— Pallas's looms stand idle, / and the spun wool slips from between my very hands. Source Probably Seneca, Phaedra (unverified)Notes Phaedra speaking. Pallas (Minerva) presides over weaving. pensa is the day's allotted wool for spinning.
trans. No rest, no work was sweet to me. In my heart’s sickness / The senses were numb, and the mind buried in torpor; / It had murdered my love of singing … g
moreNo rest, no labor, pleased my love-sick breast, My faculties were asleep, my mind was dull, I lost my zest for poesy and song. djNo rest was sweet to me, no work to my sick / heart; my senses were sluggish, my mind buried in torpor, / my zeal for song had died. — Source Burton cites Mantuan, Eclogues (unverified)Notes Faustus speaking, in Mantuan's second eclogue.
trans. this beard’s a mess, and the hair’s filthy g
moreand this beard is unkempt, and my hair filthy Source Burton cites Theocritus, Idylls, 14 (unverified)Notes A Latin rendering of the lovesick man's neglect in Theocritus, Idyll 14.
Author trans. “Why art thou so sad man”
literalwhy are you sad?
Author trans. “Whence comest”
literalWhere have you come from?
Author trans. “I have so forgotten myself, I neither know where I am, nor whence I come, nor whether I will, what I do”
literalBy Hercules, I don't know where I'm coming from or where I'm going, I have so utterly forgotten myself
trans. … In full awareness and knowledge, / alive and alert, I’m dying, and I don’t know what to do. g
moreLiving, I die, and know not what I do. dj— Knowingly and wittingly, / alive and with my eyes open, I perish, and I don't know what to do. Source Burton cites Terence, Eunuchus (unverified)Notes In Terence's play these words are spoken by Phaedria, not by Chaerea.
trans. To whom, alone, all that was knowable was revealed, g
moreTo whom alone was known whatever is knowable,"^ djTo whom alone lay open whatever could be known, Source Burton cites Epitaph of Peter Abelard (unverified)
A line from Abelard's epitaph. Author trans. “he had no mind to visit or frequent Schools and Scholars any more”
literalIt was very wearisome to me
trans. It was very irksome for me … to go to the schools, or to stay in them g
moreto go to the schools, or to stay in them Source Burton cites Peter Abelard, Letters, 1 (unverified)Notes Completes 'Taediosum mihi valde fuit' ('It was very wearisome to me').
trans. who can legislate for love? g
morewho can set bounds to love djWho can lay down a law for love? Source Burton cites Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, lib. 3 Met. ult. (unverified)
Boethius writes 'Quis legem det amantibus?' ('Who can give a law to lovers?'), followed by 'Love is a greater law unto itself'. Burton has Amori. trans. against the world g
moreagainst all the world djagainst all the world Notes A set phrase meaning 'against all comers', i.e. whatever anyone says.
Author trans. “as a reward of his worth and service”
literalthe spoil of his valour
trans. Only to will and not to will whatever your mistress wills or does not will.
moreSource Burton cites Ercole Strozzi, Epigrams (unverified)Notes A compressed line. 'velit nolit' is read as 'wills or nills', so the lover's will follows his mistress's. In the preceding paragraph Burton introduces it with 'to will and nill the same'.
trans. melancholics g
moremelancholy, djblack-bilious Notes atrabilarii: people dominated by black bile, i.e. melancholics.
Author trans. “Jupiter himself cannot love and be wise both together”
literalTo love and to be wise at once is not granted even to Jupiter himself.
trans. Whoever loves is a slave; he follows his beloved as a captive, / He bears the yoke with a tamed neck … g
moreWhoever loves is a slave, his beloved's captive, Wearing the yoke tamely upon his neck, djWhoever loves is a slave; a captive, he follows the one he loves, / And bears the yoke on a tamed neck — Source Burton cites Mantuan (unverified)Notes Burton breaks off mid-sentence.
trans. She starts to speak, and stops mid-flow. g
moreShe begins to speak, and stops short in the middle of a word. Source Burton cites Virgil, Aeneid, 4 (unverified)Notes Dido, unable to say what she feels for Aeneas.
trans. What reason asks for, passion conquers and rules, / And dominates the whole soul as a mighty god. g
moreWhat reason demands, frenzy overcomes and reigns over, / And the mighty god holds sway over my whole mind. Source Burton cites Seneca, Hippolytus (Phaedra) (unverified)
The standard text of Seneca's Phaedra reads 'quid ratio possit? vicit ac regnat furor' ('What can reason do? Frenzy has conquered and reigns'). Burton's 'Quod ratio poscit, vincit' changes the sense, and the translation follows Burton. The 'god' is Cupid. trans. O delusion, love and fury of an unhinged mind, / Where have you taken me? g
more(ovid) Beguiling love, and passion, what a gate You've led me I djO deceit, and love, and frenzy of a mind thrown off balance, / Where have you carried me off to? Source Burton cites George Buchanan, Medea (unverified)Notes From George Buchanan's Latin version of Euripides' Medea.
Author trans. “void of sense”
literalsenseless
trans. Whoever loves a frog, thinks the frog is Diana. g
moreWho loves a frog, thinks the frog as fair as Diana. djWhoever loves a frog thinks the frog is Diana. Notes A proverbial jingle: ranam ('frog') rhymes with Dianam ('Diana'), and the rhyme cannot be kept in English.
trans. wide- and snub-nosed g
moresnub-nose with wide nostrils, djwith a snub and spreading nose Notes simus means flat or snub-nosed; patulus means broad or spreading.
Author trans. “her dugs like two double jugs”
literalwith drooping breasts g
trans. you imagine whatever’s hidden to be more beautiful g
more(suppose, as the poet saith, her unseen beauties somewhat better), djif any parts lie hidden, suppose them better Source Probably Ovid, Metamorphoses, 1.502 (unverified)
Adapted from Ovid, where Apollo, looking at Daphne, 'thinks' (putat) that her hidden parts are better. Burton changes the verb to the imperative puta, 'suppose', and so turns it into ironic advice to the reader. trans. an antidote for love g
morethe very antidote of love dja cure for love Notes The phrase recalls the title of Ovid's Remedia Amoris: the woman is so repulsive that the sight of her would cure any other man of love.
trans. … These very things / delight him, like Balbinus with Hagna’s polyp, g
more— these very things / delight him, as Hagna's polyp delights Balbinus, Source Burton cites Horace, Satires, ser. lib. 1 Sat. 3 (unverified)Notes Horace's lover Balbinus is charmed even by the polyp, a fleshy growth in the nose, of his mistress Hagna. Burton leaves out the opening 'illi' ('him').
trans. This one here will surpass the face of Helen, / Which inspired terrible war. g
moreHer beauty beats Helen's, who did inspire The Trojan War, dj(She will surpass the face of Tyndareus' daughter, / which stirred up horrid wars. Source Burton cites Seneca, Octavia (unverified)Notes Tyndareus' daughter is Helen, whose face caused the Trojan War. The opening parenthesis is Burton's own.
trans. … laughing, Caelia is Venus; / Walking, she’s Juno; talking, she’s Minerva. g
more— Caelia laughing / is Venus, walking is Juno, speaking is Minerva. Source Burton cites Angerianus (unverified)
trans. whatever you say will be inadequate, etc. g
morewhatever you say will fall short, etc. Source Burton cites Petronius, Satyricon (unverified)
trans. second to none g
moresecond to none, djsecond to none Notes A common Latin phrase.
trans. … Softer than rabbit’s fur, etc. g
moresofter than a coney's fur, &c. dj— Softer than a rabbit's fur, etc. Source Probably Catullus, Carmina, 25.1 (unverified)
In Catullus this phrase mocks the effeminate Thallus. Burton reapplies it to the mistress. Author trans. “Fine Lydia my Mistress white and fair”
literalLovely Lydia, fair-skinned girl,
Author trans. “The milk, the Lily do not thee come near;”
literalwho far surpass milk and the lily,
Author trans. “The Rose so white, the Rose so red to see,”
literaland the white rose together with the red,
Author trans. “And Indian Ivory comes short of thee”
literaland polished Indian ivory
trans. And clearly it’s pure jealousy that spurs you on, / Because Polyphemus doesn’t love you as he does me; g
morePlainly 'tis envy prompts, since he Doth not love you as he doth me. djAnd plainly sheer envy seems to goad you to this, / because Polyphemus does not love you as he loves me; Source Burton cites Johannes Secundus, verse rendering of Lucian's dialogue of Doris and Galatea (unverified)Notes Galatea answering Doris in Johannes Secundus's verse version of Lucian's Dialogues of the Sea-Gods.
trans. if Augustus, the emperor of the world, wanted to marry me, g
moreIf Augustus, emperor of the world, sought me for his wife, I would rather be your whore than empress of the world. Source Burton cites Heloise, Letter to Peter Abelard (unverified)Notes This is a loose and shortened version of Heloise's letter to Abelard. In her original she says it would seem dearer and worthier to her to be called his whore than the empress of Augustus, ruler of the whole world. Burton adds the jingle 'meretrix … imperatrix' ('whore … empress').
trans. … Not even if Jupiter himself should come to want me … g
more— not even if Jupiter himself should happen to want me, — Notes A fragment cut off at both ends. 'Velit' (should want) probably means 'should want me as his wife'. Burton's sentence after it gives the sense.
Author trans. “take mine eyes, and thou wilt think she is a Goddess”
literalTake my eyes, and you will think her a goddess.
trans. No indeed: even his girlfriend’s dung doesn’t stink g
moreIndeed, not even his sweetheart's dung stinks. Notes A coarse proverbial saying: to the lover, nothing about the beloved is offensive.
trans. nor those beautiful images of Venus or Stratonice g
morenor is this the likeness of fair Cypris or of Stratonice
Cypris is Venus. Stratonice was a famously beautiful Hellenistic queen, whom Burton swaps for 'the Spanish Infanta'. trans. little heart, little kiss, etc. g
moreLittle Heart, Little Kiss, &c., djlittle heart, little kiss, etc. Notes Latin diminutive pet names: corculum from cor (heart), suaviolum from suavium (kiss). Burton calls them "pretty diminutives" but does not translate them.
trans. My honey, my lovely, my heart, / My little kiss, my sweets, g
moreMy honey, my heart, my sweetness, My rabbit, my little kiss, djMy honey, my sweetness, my heart, / my little kiss, my delights, Source Burton cites Michael Marullus, Epigrams, to Neaera, epig. 1 lib. (unverified)
trans. beautiful Margaret, all the riches of the world seem worthless compared to her g
morebeautiful Margaret, beside whom all the precious things of the world are worthless Source Burton cites Caspar Barth (unverified)
Margareta also suggests margarita, 'pearl', which sets up the comparison with the world's other 'precious things'. trans. Oh, such fingers, what a hand she has! g
moreO such fingers on that hand of hers djOh, what fingers, what hands she has!
trans. She has a thousand costumes, and wears a thousand gracefully. g
moreShe wears a thousand dresses In a thousand charming ways, djShe has a thousand fashions of dress, and wears all thousand becomingly. Source Burton cites Tibullus (unverified)
From the Sulpicia poems in the Tibullan collection (4.2.14). Author trans. “Let her wear what she will, do what she will, say what she will”
literal'tis all becoming. dj
Author trans. “let her be dressed or undressed, all is one, she is excellent still, beautiful, fair, and lovely to be behold”
literalShe puts on her clothes, and she is beautiful; she takes them off, and she is all beauty.
Author trans. “his Mistress’ servant, her drudge, prisoner, bondman”
literalthe lover, slave of his girlfriend g
Author trans. “I account this man a very drudge”
literalI reckon this man the most worthless of slaves
trans. I’ll come myself as your partner; the rugged rocks / Won’t trouble me, nor the fearsome boar’s skewed tusk, g
moreI myself will come as your companion; the rugged rocks shall not deter me, / Nor the boar, to be feared for his slanting tusk. Source Probably Ovid, Heroides, 4 (unverified)Notes Phaedra's words to Hippolytus, as Burton's next words say.
Author trans. “nothing so boisterous, nothing so tender as love”
literalNothing is softer than love, nothing more violent.
trans. He’s not deterred by the dead of night g
moreBy unseasonable night he is not deterred, djHe is not deterred by the dead of night. Notes Intempesta nox means the dead of night, the hours unfit for any business.
trans. he’ll force his way into everything, will break through everything g
morepenetrate all, overthrow all, djHe will get through everything, he will break through everything.
trans. mountains seem eminently climbable, rivers seem swimmable g
moreMountains seem easy going, rivers fit to swim.
trans. He’s prepared to pass through fire and billowing seas / And whirling winds … g
moreHe is ready to pass through fire, the waves of the sea, and the whirlwinds / Of the wind — Source Burton cites Plutarch, Amatorius (Dialogue on Love) (unverified)Notes The line breaks off in mid-sentence, as Burton's dash shows.
trans. Faunus came through the shadows to the dewy caves g
moreDew-drenched through the darkness Faunus came to the grotto, dj(Through the darkness Faunus comes to the dewy caves) Notes Faunus, the rustic god, here stands for the lover who goes out at night.
trans. I’ll surrender myself to Thais and do what she commands g
moreI give myself to Thais, djI will give myself up to Thais, and do what she bids. Source Burton cites Terence, Eunuchus, Act 5, Scene 8 (unverified)
trans. not caring about the discomforts of a long journey g
moreuncaring for the troubles of a long voyage. djnot caring for the hardships of a long voyage
trans. would you choose how you’d like him to be killed? g
moresaying to her, Choose how^ you will have him killed. djChoose by what kind of death you would have him killed. Source Burton cites Fernando de Rojas, Celestina, Act 15 & 18 (unverified)Notes Centurio's offer to Areusa. Burton quotes the Spanish Celestina in Latin.
trans. Her death will end my desires, as I die, g
moreWhen she dies, my love shall likewise be at rest in the tomb. ( BUCHANAN) djShe, dying, shall end my loves as I die with her. Source Burton cites George Buchanan (unverified)
trans. … I’d love to live with you, I’d gladly die with you. g
moreGladly Vd live with thee, or gladly die. dj— With you I would love to live, with you I would gladly die. Source Burton cites Horace, Odes (unverified)
trans. Spare me as I hurry to her; drown me when I return. g
moreSpare me while I go, overwhelm me returning, djSpare me while I hasten; drown me when I return. Source Burton cites Martial, Liber spectaculorum (On the Spectacles), epigram on Leander (unverified)
Leander's plea to the waves as he swims to Hero. Martial's text is usually printed 'mergite cum redeo'. The difference does not change the sense. trans. for them, indeed, neither wild beasts, nor fire, nor precipice, nor sea, nor sword, nor noose seem troublesome g
morecaring neither for wild beasts, nor fire, nor precipices, nor straits, nor of weapons, nor of heavy seas: djfor to them neither wild beast, nor fire, nor precipice, nor sea, nor sword, nor halter seems grievous Source Burton cites Maximus of Tyre (unverified)Notes 'Tyrius' is Maximus of Tyre. Burton names him right after this phrase, but the attribution may refer only to the clause that follows. 'Laqueus' means a noose or halter.
trans. He doesn’t fear death: he wants to march / … on to the swords themselves g
moreHe fears not death, nay, he desires to run Upon the very swords, djHe does not fear death; he longs to go / — to meet the very swords head-on Notes Burton's dash marks an omission in the middle of the quotation.
Author trans. “miserable man that I am (instead of other devotions), he cries out”
literalAlas, wretched me! he exclaims
Author trans. “so love triumphs, contemns, insults over death itself”
literalThus love … death
Author trans. “to make his corrival do as much”
literalchallenging his rival to match him in this
trans. with headwinds g
morewith adverse winds, djagainst contrary winds
trans. And Venus is honoured more with these things than with frankincense and oblations g
moreAnd by these Venus is worshipped more than by incense and sacrificial victims Source Burton cites Aristaenetus, Letters, Epist. 17 lib. 2 (unverified)
trans. For if what you love is absent, its image yet remains, / And its sweet name rings in your ears. g
moreFor if what you love is absent, still its images are at hand, / and its sweet name hovers about your ears. Source Burton cites Lucretius, De rerum natura (unverified)
trans. And a token snatched from an arm, / Or a coyly resisting finger, g
moreSome token snatched from her arm, Or hardly resisting finger, djand a love-token snatched from her arm, / or from a finger that holds on only feebly, Source Burton cites Horace, Odes (unverified)
In Horace the girl only pretends to resist, so 'male pertinaci' means 'not really meaning to hold on'. trans. … and desperate, he presses his kisses on the doors, g
moreAnd sadly prints his kisses on the doors, dj— and, poor wretch, he plants kisses on her doors, Source Probably Lucretius, De rerum natura, 4.1179 (unverified)Notes This describes the locked-out lover at his mistress's door.
trans. You Alpine breezes, breezes from the peaceful mountains, / Take this to her … g
moreYe Alpine breezes, mountain winds. Bear her these tidings. djYou Alpine breezes, breezes from the gentle mountains, / carry these words to her. — Source Burton cites Girolamo Fracastoro, poem addressed to Andrea Navagero (unverified)Notes The dash marks where Burton breaks off the quotation.
trans. Every breeze will breathe out ambrosia. g
moreAll the air will breathe ambrosia. djEvery breeze will breathe ambrosia.
trans. a broken heart g
moreA torn heart Notes Scissum means 'cut' or 'rent'. Burton's English that follows ('bruised to powder, dissolved and melted') expands the phrase freely.
trans. Oh, if I could toy with you as she does, / And ease the sad pains of my heart! g
moreO, if I could play with you as she herself does, / and lighten the sad cares of my mind. Source Probably Catullus, Carmina, 2.9–10 (unverified)Notes Catullus is addressing Lesbia's sparrow and wishing he could play with it as she does. Burton has added the opening 'O si' to turn the lines into a wish.
Author trans. “But I a looking-glass would be,”
literalBut I myself would become a mirror,
Author trans. “Still to be lookt upon by thee,”
literalso that you might always gaze on me, your own,
Author trans. “Or I, my Love, would be thy gown,”
literaland I myself would become your garment,
Author trans. “By thee to be worn up and down;”
literalso that you might always wear me, your own.
Author trans. “Or a pure Well full to the brims,”
literalAnd I wish to be changed into water,
Author trans. “That I might wash thy purer limbs:”
literalso that I might wash your limbs,
Author trans. “Or I’d be precious balm to ’noint,”
literalgirl, I would become spikenard ointment,
Author trans. “With choicest care each choicest joint;”
literalso that I might anoint you,
Author trans. “To be the Lawn o’er thy fair pap.”
literalmay I be the band about your breasts,
Author trans. “About thy neck thy happy chain.”
literaland a necklace for your neck.
Author trans. “Or would I were thy shoe, to be”
literalAnd may I become your shoe, so that me
Author trans. “Daily but trod upon by thee.”
literalat least you might always tread with your foot.
trans. … lucky mother, etc., lucky nurse … / But far beyond them all, and far more fortunate is he, / Who delights in being your betrothed and is deemed worthy of sharing your bed. g
moreHappy thy mother, happy thy nurse, But happiest she, the bride that shares thy bed. dj— Happy the mother, etc., happy the nurse — / but far beyond all, and far more blessed, is he / whom you will deem worthy of the joys of a bridegroom and a shared bed. Source Probably Ovid, Metamorphoses, 4.322–326 (unverified)Notes Burton adapts Salmacis' speech to Hermaphroditus (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.322ff), where the line reads 'sed longe cunctis longeque beatior illa' and refers to a bride. Here it has become masculine (ille, sponsi), which suits Hero, and the last line differs from Ovid's. The opening is cut short with '&c.' The sense of 'fructu sponsi' is somewhat uncertain.
Author trans. “happy are his bedfellows”
literalTruly, fortunate are the women who sleep with him,
Author trans. “blessed is that woman that shall be his wife”
literalBlessed is she who shall be his wife
Author trans. “such a night’s lodging is worth Jupiter’s Sceptre.”
literalOne night to be ranked equal with the sceptre of Jove,
Author trans. “O What a blissful night would it be”
literalWhat a night that will be, O gods and goddesses,
Author trans. “how soft, how sweet a bed?”
literalHow soft a bed!
trans. He who sees you is blessed; / More blessed is he who’ll hear you; / He who possesses you is a god. g
moreHappy is he who sees thee. Happier he who hears thee, A demigod he who kisses thee, A god he who possesses thee, djWhoever sees you is blessed, / more blessed whoever shall hear you, / whoever possesses you is a god. Source Burton cites Rufinus (unverified)Notes Burton's sidenote says the lines are Latinised from the Greek of Rufinus.
trans. … grant this last gift to a wretched lover. g
moreGrant this last favour to your hapless lover, dj— grant this last gift to a wretched lover. Source Probably Virgil, Aeneid, 4.429 (unverified)Notes Dido's words in Virgil read "det" ("let him grant"). Burton has the imperative "da" ("grant") so that the line fits the Sultan's wife pleading directly.
trans. determined to follow his precious body as a shadow does g
moreto follow the dear body, as a faithful shadow is wont to do Notes The line reads as a pentameter. Its source is not identified here.
trans. and one of the gods, not one of the dreary ones, said, etc. g
moreand one of the gods, none of the gloomy ones, says, etc. Source Probably Ovid, Metamorphoses, 4 (unverified)
This recalls Ovid's tale of Mars and Venus caught in Vulcan's net, where one of the less severe gods wishes he could be disgraced in the same way. Ovid has "optat" ("wishes"), not "inquit" ("says"). trans. … For her I shall not be afraid to die … g
more— for whom I would not fear to die — Source Burton cites Horace, Odes, Ode 9 book 3 (unverified)
Author trans. “I will die twice, nay twenty times for her”
literalfor whom I would not fear to die twice
Author trans. “Venus forsook Heaven for Adonis’ sake”
literalAdonis is preferred to heaven.
trans. love tames feral souls g
morelove tames savage breasts djdesire tames savage minds
trans. love made her bold g
moreLove made him bold. Source Burton cites Ovid, Metamorphoses (unverified)
In Ovid the words are said of Thisbe, so the original sense is "made her bold". trans. love expels fear from the breast g
morelove drives out fear. djlove drives fear out of the breast Notes "Expectorat" literally means "drives out of the breast". It is a rare, archaic verb.
trans. lest his lover might see he was wounded in the back g
morelest his lover should see him wounded in the back Source Burton cites Plutarch, Amatorius (Dialogue on Love) (unverified)Notes "Amasius" is masculine. In Plutarch's story the dying warrior is anxious about his male beloved.
trans. were the whole mass of the heavens to fall, I wouldn’t be scared, etc. g
morethough the heavens should fall, djThough the whole mass of heaven should fall, I am not afraid, etc. Source Burton cites Girolamo Angeriano (unverified)Notes The sidenote "Angerianus." probably belongs to this line, but that is not certain.
Author trans. “that famous buckler of Argos”
literalthe Argive shield
Author trans. “only Lovers”
literalonly lovers
Author trans. “only Lovers will die for their friends”
literalthey are eager to die for their friends
trans. For love inspires tricks and produces deceits, g
moreFor love inspires to stratagems and frauds, djFor love inspires tricks and supplies deceits, Source Burton cites Mantuan, Eclogues, Ecl. 1 (unverified)
Author trans. “for shelter he fled to Leda’s lap”
literaland settled himself in her lap
trans. but Jupiter had intercourse with her while she slept g
morebut he took her asleep, djbut while she slept Jupiter lay with her Source Burton cites Hyginus, Poetica Astronomica, lib. 2 (unverified)
trans. … who can deceive a lover? g
moreWho can deceive a lover? dj— who could deceive a lover? Source Burton cites Virgil, Aeneid (unverified)
In Virgil the half-line is about Dido sensing Aeneas' secret plan to leave. Burton turns it round to mean that love itself is cunning. trans. more wit and charm g
moremore wit and charm Source Probably Plautus, Casina (unverified)Notes Sal ('salt') means wit; lepos means charm or grace.
trans. love surpasses in all things, and with exquisite elegancies g
morelove is foremost in the nicenesses of elegance, djlove surpasses all things, even the brightest splendours Source Burton cites Plautus, Casina, act. 2 sc. 4 (unverified)Notes 'Nitidis nitoribus' is a Plautine jingle, roughly 'shining shinings'. The point is that love outdoes every elegance.
trans. for Venus is the mother of charms g
morefor Venus is mother of the graces; djfor Venus is the mother of charms Notes This plays on Venus and venustas ('charm, loveliness'), which comes from her name.
trans. a marriageable girl g
morea marriageable girl
Author trans. “Venetian Bride”
literalbride
trans. they strive for elegance above their means g
morebefore all things they must study to be elegant, djthey strive after elegance beyond what the occasion allows Source Burton cites Plautus (unverified)
trans. Godlike in face and shoulders, for his mother / Had herself imparted to her son beautiful hair, / A rosy glow of youth and a joyful charm to his eyes. g
more(Like a god in face and shoulders; for his mother herself had breathed upon her son / graceful locks, and the radiant bloom of youth, / and a joyful lustre in his eyes.) Source Probably Virgil, Aeneid, 1.589–591 (unverified)
trans. I’m not so hideous; I saw myself recently on the shore, / When the sea stood becalmed from the winds … g
moreI am not so ugly; lately I saw myself on the shore, / when the sea lay calm, stilled by the winds — Source Burton cites Virgil, Eclogues, Ecl. 2 (unverified)Notes Corydon is speaking. The sentence is broken off mid-line.
trans. scrubbed clean g
morefaultless as a lotus, djcleanly washed Notes Lotus is a variant spelling of lautus, 'washed, smart'.
Author trans. “combed and curled”
literalcombed and curled
trans. for it didn’t permit the joining of pure to pure, and so to sweeter, lips g
morefor because of it I could not join lips to lips, clean to clean, and so all the sweeter Source Burton cites Julian the Apostate, Misopogon (unverified)Notes The syntax is compressed. The sense is that the beard kept him from pressing clean lips to clean lips, which is sweeter. The Latin is a translation of Julian's Greek.
trans. I don’t care about getting or giving kisses g
moreI do not exert myself, said he, in the giving and taking of kisses; djI do not trouble myself about taking or giving kisses Source Burton cites Julian the Apostate, Misopogon (unverified)
trans. A boy barber, but of such skill, / As not even Nero’s Thalamus was; g
moreA barber, a boy, but so skilled in his craft / as not even Nero's Thalamus was; Source Burton cites Martial, Epigrams, 5 (unverified)Notes Thalamus was Nero's famous barber. The lines are in the accusative and depend on a verb that Burton leaves out; he is listing what a suitor must keep about him.
Author trans. “Love will make them Musicians, and to compose ditties, Madrigals, Elegies, Love Sonnets”
literalLove teaches music and poetry
Author trans. “all to ingratiate himself, and please his Mistress”
literalso that he might please the maiden
Author trans. “but his mother Venus danced to his and their sweet content”
literalbut Venus, stepping in to the sweet music, danced
trans. … So dies the youth; so dying, still he loves. g
moreTherefore youth dies, therefore the near-dead love, dj— So the young man dies, so the dying man loves. Source Burton cites Joach. Bellius, Epigrams (unverified)Notes Only the last line of the epigram is quoted; it ends the fable of Cupid and Death exchanging arrows. 'Bellius' is probably Joachim du Bellay.
Author trans. “how love makes them that had no skill before, learn to sing and dance”
literalLove teaches music, even to one who was unskilled before
trans. two hundred thousand drachmas for a single night g
moretwo hundred drachmas for a single night, djtwo hundred thousand drachmas for a single night Source Burton cites Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, lib. 18 cap. 4 (unverified)
trans. due to the abundance of semen, repeated thoughts and frequent recollection of sex, and tickling pleasure, etc. g
morebecause of an abundance of seed come frequent thoughts, constant recollection of love's pleasures, and an itching desire, etc. Source Burton cites Giulio Guastavini (Guastavinius), Commentary on the Aristotelian Problems, 4 Sect. 27 (unverified)Notes The physiological explanation follows the humoral theory of the time. 'Veneris' refers to sexual love (Venus).
trans. a tingling body, a tingling soul g
moreitching body, itching mind, djan itching body, an itching soul
trans. How would life be now, or what pleasure would there be, without golden Venus? I’d die if I no longer cared for those things g
morewhat would life be worth, or what pleasure without Venus? djWhat life would there be now, or what delight, without golden Venus? May I die when these things are no longer my care. Source Burton cites Mimnermus (unverified)
A Latin version of Mimnermus' Greek elegy ('What is life, what is delight, without golden Aphrodite? May I die…'). Burton's English renders only the second sentence, and loosely. trans. when love is absent, up spring shadows, torpor, lethargy, pestilence, etc. g
morewhen love goes, the shadows gather, old age with its stiff joints, disease, &c. djTake love away, and there arise darkness, torpor, lethargy, plague, etc. Source Burton cites Girolamo Angeriano (Angerianus) (unverified)Notes The sidenote 'Angerianus.' (the neo-Latin love poet Girolamo Angeriano) probably belongs to this line, but that cannot be confirmed. Veternus is the sluggish torpor of lethargy.
Author trans. “for love’s sake”
literalby the kindness of love
Author trans. “to comfort herself in his absence”
literalso that she would pine away less with desire for him g
trans. they would never have discovered such things if they hadn’t desired them deeply g
moreNever had they found out such things, had they not loved djThey would never have invented such things had they not loved such things. Notes The jingle sets invenissent ('they had invented') against adamassent ('they had fallen in love with').
trans. Nobility lies subject to love … g
moreNobility lies subject to love — Notes A broken-off half-line. It sits inside Burton's sentence 'All our Tilts and Tournaments, Orders of the Garter… owe their beginnings to love'. The exact sense of 'sub amore jacet' (lies beneath, depends on, or is subject to love) is uncertain without the rest of the verse.
trans. they owe it to love that they’re read and praised g
morethat they are read, that they are praised, they owe to love Source Burton cites Giovanni Nevizzano (Nevisanus), Sylva nuptialis, Lib. 4 num. 102 (unverified)
trans. Thracian Orpheus won’t conquer me in song, / Neither will Linus. g
more(martial) Not Thracian Orpheus shall vanquish me in song. Nor Linus, djNeither Thracian Orpheus shall outdo me in songs, / nor Linus. Source Burton cites Virgil, Eclogues, Ecl. 4 (unverified)Notes Virgil, Eclogue 4.55–56. The standard text reads 'vincat' and 'Thracius', where Burton has 'vincet' and 'Thraceus'. The quotation breaks off after 'Linus'.
trans. levities, enticements, jokes, grace, nard, spring, garland, incense, Mars, Athena, Venus, Grace, saffron, laurel, perfume, costus, tears, myrrh, Muses, etc. g
moreprofligacies, flatteries, jests, elegance. Spikenard, Spring, Garland, Frankincense, Mars, Pallas, Venus, Grace, Saffron, Laurel, Perfume, Costum [the herb Zedoary] , Tears, Myrrh, the Muses, djNaughtinesses, Blandishments, Jests, Grace, Nard, Spring, Garland, Frankincense, Mars, Pallas, Venus, Charis, Saffron, Laurel, Ointment, Costus, Tears, Myrrh, Muses, etc. Source Burton cites Giovanni Pontano (unverified)Notes These read as the titles or subjects of Pontanus' love poems, so they are given as titles. Charis, the Grace, is kept as a name. Costus is an aromatic root. Nequitiae could also be rendered 'wantonnesses'.
trans. who stink of horse dung g
morestinking of horse-dirt, djwho stink of horse dung

literallet this city supply the woman's headband, this one her neck-ornaments, this one her hair
Author trans. “ignorant in all arts, and sciences”
literaland though he disclaimed knowledge of all other things
Author trans. “a Doctor alone in love matters”
literala professor of this business, etc.
trans. in the Piraeus, the Lyceum, under the plane tree, etc. g
morein the Piraeus, the Lyceum, under the plane trees, &c.. djin the Piraeus, in the Lyceum, under the plane tree, etc. Source Burton cites Maximus of Tyre, Dissertations, Serm. 8 (unverified)
These are places where Socrates held his conversations. The plane tree recalls the setting of Plato's Phaedrus. trans. I don’t know what love is, nor do I love … g
moreI know not what love is, nor do I love — Notes The line breaks off at Burton's dash. Burton uses it to claim, half in jest, that he has no experience of love, and he qualifies the claim straight away in the next sentence.
trans. I’m a man, etc. g
moreI am a man, etc. Source Probably Terence, Heauton Timorumenos, 77 (unverified)
Burton cuts the line short. In full it reads 'homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto': 'I am a man; I count nothing human foreign to me.' Here it serves as his excuse for knowing something about love. trans. I’m not an instructor in loving g
moreI am not a teacher of love, djI am no teacher of loving
This seems to turn around Ovid's boast in the Art of Love that he was a 'praeceptor Amoris', a teacher of Love. The wording here is not certainly Ovid's. trans. from others’ absurdities perhaps g
morethe follies of others, djdrawn perhaps from the follies of others Notes Burton adds 'drawn' to make the phrase fit his sentence: what he says comes from reading, and perhaps from other people's foolishness in love.
