encounter; combat; disturbance; passion w gloss apaid Paid; pleased w gloss belike It is likely or probably; perhaps w gloss chiefest First or foremost; chief; principal w gloss belike It is likely or probably; perhaps w gloss facete Facetious; witty; humorous w note green sickness Chlorosis: a disease thought to afflict young, virginal women, causing a greenish discoloration of the skin and other symptoms.about Cachexia A general sickness of the body involving deficient nutrition.gloss habit Physical condition or constitution.source son-in-law The unnamed second wife of the owner of the narrator Lucius’ lodging, who has fallen in love with her stepson (Metamorphoses 10.3).note blushed besides This apocryphal tale, taken from Plutarch’s Life of Demetrius (38) and involving the ancient Greek anatomist and physician Erasistratus, was frequently recycled in the Renaissance. Seleucus I – see above, – did marry the famously beautiful Stratonice in his old age, but his personal doctor was actually Erasistratus’ father Cleombrotus.source Pulse and Countenance A conflation of Galen’s account (On Prognosis 8.21) of his cure of the wife of one of his patrons, Flavius Boethus, who was suffect consul before 163 CE, with the same author’s story about Pylades and the wife of Justin – see above, .note as Poliarchus did at the name of Argenis In John Barclay’s novel Argenis (1621), Poliarchus is one of the suitors of the princess Argenis; their eventual marriage restores stability to the kingdom.about Maiden blush A delicate shade of pink.about Come kiss me Corinna A slight misquotation of the comedy Τεχνογαμία, or The Marriages of the Arts (1618) by the poet Barten Holiday, which had been performed at Christ Church in February 1617 when its author was a Student there. The name ‘Corinna’, which was frequently used in Renaissance love poetry, alludes to the narrator’s beloved in Ovid’s Loves.source Philippides her in Aristaenetus In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (1.16), it is actually the character of Lamprias, confessing to his friend Philippides, who has enjoyed a kiss with his (unnamed) beloved.gloss saluted Kissed, or greeted with a kiss.about inserere Chremes, addressing his son Clitipho in Terence’s Self-Tormentor (863–4).about Ixion In classical mythology, when Jupiter (Zeus) brought the Thessalian king Ixion to Olympus, the latter attempted to assault Juno (Hera) indecently; but Jupiter tricked Ixion into having intercourse with a cloud made in her shape instead.note as Apollo on Leucothoe In classical mythology, the sun-god Helios (Sol), sometimes identified as Phoebus Apollo, fell in love with the Persian princess Leucothoe and raped her.source the Moon … Chariot to be stayed See above, . This quotation from Lucian’s Dialogues of the Gods (19.1) refers to the Latmus mountain range, of which Endymion was the local hero, in Caria.gloss Adamant Loadstone.source Aristaenetus of Euxitheus In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (2.2), Euxitheus declares his love for Pythias, whom has met while praying in a temple.gloss wistly Intently.source The Sultan of Sana’s wife in Arabia According to Ludovico di Varthema (Vertomannus), he had actually been imprisoned by the Sultan of Rada’a (now a district in Yemen), who left him in charge of one of his wives while on a military campaign against the Sultan of Sana’a. Varthema says that he subsequently feigned madness, and managed to escape by persuading the sultan’s wife to let him visit a physician to treat him.gloss hem Clear the throat (here, to attract attention).source Demophoon were approaching In Ovid’s Heroides (2.1–2), the mythical Thracian princess Phyllis (‘Rhodopeia’ in the quotation refers to the Rhodope mountain range in western Thrace) addresses her beloved, the king of Athens Demophoon (or Demophon).source Troilus to the City gates … Criseyde A passage from Virgil’s Aeneid (1.475), where Aeneas is viewing a painting of the Trojan War, and sees the image of Troilus, the young Trojan prince who was ambushed and killed by Achilles (and whose romance with Chryseis, a medieval invention, was the subject of Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde and Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida).gloss kens Looks, scans.about as he calls it in the poet Alcesimarchus, a young man from Sicyon who has fallen in love with Silenium, in Plautus’ Casket Comedy (203–10).about lovesick son Terence, in his Brothers (696–8).source Theocles prays In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (2.8), Theocles has fallen in love with his mother-in-law.gloss gales Talk, speeches.about such delight In the Comedia de Calisto y Melibea (1499), widely known as La Celestina, by Fernando de Rojas, the young man Calisto attempts to seduce Melibea, the daughter of a local nobleman, with the help of a procuress called Celestina; the story features two of Calisto’s servants, called Sosia (also the name of a female slave in several Roman comedies) and Tristan.note repentance dwell Note ‘c’ is a quotation from the English poet and translator Robert Tofte’s Blazon of Jealousie (1615) – itself a version of the Lettura sopra un sonetto della gelosia di mons. Dalla Casa (1545) by the Italian humanist scholar Benedetto Varchi; the note was present only in the first edition of 1621, but has here been restored. The omission in later versions was probably due to an error by the 1624 compositor, who had to deal with extensive additions to this part of the text. Burton rarely removed material from new editions without an obvious reason.gloss castaway Reprobate, someone rejected.note careful Amyntas Amyntas is the shepherd beloved of Menalcas in Virgil’s Eclogues.gloss stool-ball A rural game similar to cricket, played mainly by young women.gloss barley-break A flirtatious game of ‘catch’, in which one couple chases two other couples.about the Elysian fields In Elysium, the paradise for the righteous which had traditionally been set aside for heroes in ancient Greek religion, and which is described at the end of Plato’s Republic.gloss stern Rudder, or helm.note our Herbalists call Narcissus The ‘tulipant’ (tulip) was sometimes referred to in contemporary botany as ‘narcissus’ because of its apparent propensity to hide its flowers at sunset or in poor weather conditions (putatively echoing the shy retreat of the mythical Narcissus from the attentions of the nymph Echo). Carolus Gonzaga,source Duke of Mantua According to the Imprese illustri (1584) of Girolamo Ruscelli, the emblem of Carlo Gonzaga (d. 1456) was accompanied by the Spanish motto ‘Syn sus rayos mys desmayos’ (‘Without its rays I faint’).about Impress Here, the image produced by a seal or stamp – see also above, .gloss inamorates Lovers.about Primum mobile In the Ptolemaic astronomy whose influence persisted into the Renaissance, the ‘spheres’ were the eight concentric, transparent and hollow globes thought to revolve round the earth, with each carrying the sun, moon, planets and fixed stars. Some added a ninth clear, ‘crystalline’ sphere above the fixed stars, and a tenth sphere of the primum mobile, said to set the other spheres in motion.note anima informans Literally, ‘informing soul’, or ‘soul giving form’. In scholastic philosophy, the ‘form’ is the essential determinant of matter, which actualizes its potentiality – as in the common definition of the soul as the ‘form of the living body’: see above, .note Cynosure, Hesperus & Vesper, his morning and evening Star ‘Cynosure’ is the Pole Star; ‘Hesperus’ and ‘Vesper’ are both names for the evening star, the planet Venus in the evening; and the ‘morning star’ is the same planet in the morning. The description of the beloved as a celestial body is common trope in classical erotic literature.about His Laura An allusion to Laura (probably Laura de Noves, 1310–48), the beloved of Petrarch in his poetry.source illapsus The original source of the quotation in note ‘b’, the Punica (15.94–5) of Silius Italicus, refers to the power of ‘Voluptas’ (Pleasure), who is portrayed in a struggle with ‘Virtus’ (Virtue). Burton has substituted Juno as the Roman goddess of love and marriage.source consume himself According to Philostratus (Life of Apollonius of Tyana 1.36), the courtier, who had slept with one of the wives of the Parthian king Vardanes I (d. 45 CE), was a eunuch. Apollonius – on whom, see above, – counselled that the pain of continuing to live with frustrated desire would itself be the right punishment.gloss flux A discharge of blood or excrement, often in relation to dysentery.note accede ad hanc ignem The ungrammatical substitution of the feminine pronoun hanc for the masculine hunc, found in some versions of Terence’s Eunuch (85), suggests that the ‘flame’ (ignis) being referred to is the courtesan Thais.gloss inextinguible Inextinguishable.note 100,000 bodies The comparison with the Neronian conflagration in 64 CE is drawn by the courtly lover Calisto in the first act of Rojas’s Celestina.about Empedocles A Presocratic philosopher (c. 492–432 BCE) from Acragas (Agrigento) in Sicily, who was famous for his two poems On Nature and Purifications.gloss sod Boiled.see 1.1.2.5note the shepherd in Theocritus The lovesick Aeschinas, in Idylls 14.gloss flag Drooping, pendulous.gloss pranking Dress ostentatiously, decorate.gloss amort Lifeless, dejected.gloss Schools Universities.gloss dizzards Idiots, blockheads.gloss precipitates Hurls down into a bad position, ruins.note Jupiter into a Bull In classical mythology, Europa, daughter of the Phoenician king Agenor, was abducted by Zeus (Jupiter) when he turned himself into (or sent) a bull to entice her; Amymone, one of the daughters of Danaus, was rescued from a satyr and seduced by Poseidon (Neptune).about Apuleius an Ass In Apuleius’ Metamorphoses, the protagonist Lucius (named after the author) accidentally turns himself into an ass.note Lycaon a wolf In the classical myth related by Pausanias, the Arcadian king Lycaon was turned into a wolf by Zeus (Jupiter) as a punishment for testing the god’s omniscience by sacrificing a baby on an altar dedicated to him. In Ovid’s version, the punishment is for plotting to murder Jupiter and, when that failed, to feed human flesh to him.about Tereus a Lapwing The mythical Thracian king Tereus was turned into a hoopoe (often confused with lapwings in the Middle Ages and Renaissance) as a punishment by the gods for raping Philomela, the sister of his wife Procne. The sisters were turned into a swallow and a nightingale, after Procne had retaliated by killing her son Itys and feeding him to Tereus.about Callisto a Bear There are different explanations in classical mythology for the transformation of Callisto, an Arcadian nymph (or princess, and daughter of Lycaon) into a bear. In some accounts it is a punishment by Artemis (Diana), or Hera (Juno), for losing her virginity after falling in love with Zeus (Jupiter) and being seduced or raped by him; in others, she is turned into a bear by Zeus in order to conceal his deed from Hera. She is also said to have become the constellation of the Great Bear after being killed by Artemis.note An immodest woman is like a Bear Note ‘a’ draws on the association, common since the Middle Ages, of bears with violent lust. The bear was also a traditional symbol of unchastity.note Elpenor and Gryllus … Circe Drawing on the tenth book of the Odyssey, in which the companions of Odysseus (Ulysses) were transformed by Circe into animals, Plutarch’s Gryllus describes Odysseus’ attempt to restore them to human form, and relates the argument of Gryllus (now a pig) that animals have greater virtue and intelligence than humans. Elpenor, the youngest companion of Odysseus, is not mentioned in the dialogue.note se redeat The allusion to Apuleius’ Metamorphoses in note ‘b’ refers to the crown of roses eaten by Lucius in a religious ceremony, which transforms him back into human form at the end of the novel.gloss tallow-faced Pale or yellowish-white faced.note a swollen Juggler’s platter face A broad, round, flat face with puffed-out cheeks, like a face pulled by a jester or buffoon.gloss chitty Lean and pinched.gloss clouds Dark spots.gloss squized Squeezed or squashed.gloss sparrow-mouthed Wide-mouthed.gloss gubber-tushed With large projecting teeth.note Bavarian poke Or ‘Bavarian poke’: goitre, prevalent throughout the Alpine region.gloss lave-eared With drooping or hanging ears.gloss bloody-fallen fingers Fingers with sores, pustules or ulcerated chilblains.note aufe A goblin child, or a changeling left by the fairies (and so a misbegotten, deformed child, or a simpleton).gloss savours Stinks.gloss incondite Crude, unrefined.gloss tit A disreputable young woman.gloss fustilugs A gross, foul-smelling woman.gloss truss A baggy, shapeless person.gloss raw-bone A very thin or gaunt person.gloss sneaker A shifty, stealthy person.gloss mard Turd.gloss rammy Rank, pungent.about Irus’ daughter Daughter of a poor man – on Irus, see above, .source Thersites’ sister According to Homer (Iliad 2.211–77), a lame, abusive and exceedingly ugly Greek soldier in the Trojan War.about Grobian’s scholar A coarse, crude person (in Renaissance satire, ‘St Grobian’ was the fictional patron saint of the vulgarly ill-mannered).gloss carrack Galleon.gloss caskanet An ornamental collar or necklace, a carcanet.gloss myriads of crowns Innumerable coins (or, more strictly, tens of thousands of them).about Burgundy A list of famously beautiful (and/or wealthy) queens: on Panthea, see above, ; Cleopatra VII of Egypt; Tanaquil, according to Roman tradition, was the noble Etruscan wife of Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of Rome; Mariamme I (b. 53/2 BCE) was the beautiful second wife of Herod the Great; Mary, Duchess of Burgundy (1457–82 CE), the daughter of Charles the Bold (‘Carolus Pugnax’ in note ‘b’), was sometimes known as ‘Mary the Rich’.about Larissean Coronis In classical mythology, the famously beautiful princess, daughter of Phlegyas (king of the Lapiths), beloved of Apollo and mother of Asclepius. Apollo kills her after discovering through a raven, his messenger, that she has slept with Ischys.about Babylonian Thisbe The mythical tragic tale of these beautiful Babylonian lovers is told in the fourth book of Ovid’s Metamorphoses.about Polyxena In Greek mythology, Polyxena was the youngest daughter of King Priam of Troy and Queen Hecuba. Some ancient sources identify Polyxena as the beloved of Achilles, who is said to have fallen for her either at the negotiations for the ransom of the body of Hector, or while spying on her brother Troilus.about Laura An allusion to Laura (probably Laura de Noves, 1310–48), the beloved of Petrarch in his poetry.about Lesbia Catullus’ beloved, a pseudonym for Clodia – possibly the married sister of Publius Clodius, on whom, see above, .gloss counterfeit Fictional.about Hebe In classical mythology, the daughter of Zeus (Jupiter) and Hera (Juno), and the personification of beauty in youth.source her behalf In the Erotic Letters (1.12), Euhemerus is enamoured of the courtesan Pythias, whom he presents as beautiful and virtuous.about Sea-God On this allusion and the verse immediately following, see above, .gloss Elogies Eulogies.gloss conceited Ingenious, clever.note absolute and perfect This story from a fragment of Plutarch (134) refers to the Greek painter and sculptor Zeuxis (fl. c. 435/25–390 BCE), whose painting of Helen in the temple of Hera Lacinia in Acragas (Agrigento) in Sicily was famous in antiquity, and Nicomachus (fl. c. 360–320 BCE), who was another important painter, possibly from Thebes.about British Bunduica Boudicca (or Boadicea, d. 60/61 BCE), whose name has many different spellings in this era: the queen of the Iceni, a Brittonic tribe whose territory included parts of East Anglia.about Sostrata’s bitch The original copies of the Anatomy have ‘Sostratu’s bitch’. Given the subsequent reference to Parmeno, ‘Sostrata’, the name of the widow in Terence’s Brothers, was probably intended (although Burton possibly misremembered this as ‘Sostratus’).about Parmeno’s sow Probably a reference to the slave Parmeno from Terence’s Brothers. But it may also refer to an ancient proverbial saying about popular delusion, ‘Nothing compared to Parmeno’s sow’; according to Plutarch, this originated in the imitation of a pig’s squeal given by Parmeno (probably a comic actor), which gained more applause than that of a real pig.about Venerilla A little Venus.source Quanto quam Lucifer … Herce In note ‘a’, the quotation from Ovid (Metamorphoses 2.723–4) refers to Mercury (Hermes) falling in love with Herse, one of the daughters of the Attic king Cecrops in classical mythology.source Stratonices This quotation, a Latin translation of an epigram by the Greek poet Nicander of Colophon, alludes to the deification of Stratonice – the wife of Seleucus I Nicator – and her frequent identification with Aphrodite (Venus), in several Greek cities after her death.about Dulcinea The imaginary beloved of Cervantes’s Don Quixote.about Antiphila The beloved of Clinia in Terence’s Self-Tormentor.about Veneres Venuses (and so, beautiful or charming features).about Roscius References to the Roman statesman and poet Quintus Lutatius Catulus (c. 150–87 BCE), and the famous (and reportedly handsome) actor Quintus Roscius Gallus (d. 62), who was defended by Cicero in a civil trial.note curiously Both ‘nice’ and ‘curious’ here mean ‘fastidious’, or ‘exceedingly careful and precise’ – qualities often derogatorily attributed to contemporary puritans, who are also the ‘schismatics’ being accused here of destroying the unity of the English Church.note delight and darling In the original source, Barth’s Latin translation of Celestina (1624), Calisto actually addresses his beloved Melibea as his ‘most precious pearl’ (‘pretiosissima margarita’). In extracting and rendering the quotation, Burton substitutes ‘Margaret’, which is etymologically derived from margarita.gloss undressed Here, probably ‘casually dressed’, rather than ‘naked’.gloss fonder Foolish, silly.note parasangs An ancient Persian unit of length: the distance travelled in one hour (whether by foot or horseback, however, is uncertain), and usually thought to be approximately 3¾ miles.source beyond all others In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (1.24), the courtesan Musarium (Mousarion in Greek versions), who has been criticized by a group of suitors for restricting her affections to the unexceptional Lysias, expresses her devotion to her beloved.source Mopsus The young poet whose marriage to Nysa is celebrated in Virgil’s Eclogues (8.26–30).gloss enamorate Lover.gloss in respect In comparison.gloss congee Take ceremonious leave.about Areusa One of the prostitutes in Rojas’s Celestina.note and spun As part of his punishment for killing his host Iphitus, Hercules performed the duties of the slave for Omphale. In the Latin versions of the myth, he is forced to carry out the typically female work of spinning wool, and is sometimes said to have become her lover.note not resist An allusion to Petronius’ Satyricon (130), where Encolpius, who has assumed the identity of a slave called Polyaenus (an epithet of Odysseus), has been sexually humiliated in failing to satisfy the desire of ‘Circe’ – see above, – and attempts to redeem himself.about Areusa In Act 15, after being insulted by Areusa, the rogue Centurio says that he would prefer her to order him to kill ten men rather than travel a league on foot.about was drowned In the Morosophiae … liber alter (1620), the German scholar Gaspar Ens says that Galeatus (Galeazzo) was a Milanese merchant who lived in the time of Louis XII’s campaigns in Italy (1494–1504), and that he killed his beloved Lucretia before committing suicide.about Ticinum Now Pavia, on the River Ticino in northern Italy.source Aeolus to Juno In Virgil’s Aeneid (1.50–86), quoted after this allusion, the Homeric ruler of the winds, Aeolus, accedes to Juno’s request to send a storm that will sink Aeneas’ fleet.note hold us both In the pseudo-Lucianic Affairs of the Heart (46), the Athenian Callicratidas is actually referring to an idealized boy, as part of a speech proving the superiority of male homosexual love.about Sciron and Procrustes Two terrifying Attic bandits who ambushed travellers in Greek mythology: Sciron, who forced his victims to wash his feet before hurling them into an abyss inhabited by a human-eating turtle; and Procrustes, who tortured travellers to death by stretching them and hitting their limbs with a hammer until they fitted his enormous (‘Procrustean’) bed. Both were killed by Theseus while he was crossing the Isthmus of Corinth.note coulters The iron blades fixed in front of the share in a plough; cf. 3.3.2.1, p. 952.about Brandimarte in Barbary In Orlando furioso, Zerbino dies in the arms of Isabella, and Brandimarte expires after being mortally wounded on the island of Lipadusa (near the coast of Africa), in the middle of saying the name of his beloved wife Fiordiligi.note as Arcite did his Emily In Chaucer’s ‘Knight’s Tale’, the knight Arcite, whose last words are quoted immediately after this allusion, dies when he is thrown from his horse after winning a contest for Emily’s hand with his rival Palamon.note by a slight In Greek mythology, when a prophecy claimed that Oenomaus would be killed by his son-in-law, the king decreed that his daughter’s hand in marriage could be obtained only after defeating him in a chariot-race, in which failure meant death. Many suitors were killed, but Pelops won by sabotaging the axle of Oenomaus’ chariot.about obtained his suit In one version of her myth, the beautiful Boeotian princess is permitted to remain a virgin only if she defeats her suitors in a race. One of them, Hippomenes, wins by dropping three golden apples obtained from Aphrodite into her way during the contest.about Sabea The ancient kingdom of Sheba, whose territory lies in what is now Yemen (although Burton’s source actually states that the events occurred in a Libyan city called Silene).note the golden legend The Aurea legenda, or Legenda sanctorum, a collection of hagiographies compiled in the second half of the thirteenth century by the Italian chronicler and archbishop of Genoa, Jacopo da Voragine (1228/9–98).note the great Cham’s court Khan, the title given to the rulers of the Tartars and Mongols.see Candish See above, .source serve twice seven years … Rachel Genesis 29:18–28.source Gismunda the daughter of Tancredus … died In Decameron 4.1, Guiscardo is killed by Tancred, who sends Ghismonda his heart in a golden cup. Ghismonda pours poison into the cup and drinks it, and rather than eating the heart, she places it on top of her own as she lies down to die.about as Artemisia drank … powder Artemisia II of Caria (in western Anatolia) was famously grief-stricken when her husband (and brother) Mausolus died in 353 BCE; cf. above, .source more torments than Theseus or Paris On Theseus, see above, . In the Trojan Epic (10.223–335) by the Greek poet Quintus of Smyrna (third century CE), Paris died in prolonged agony after being shot by the Thessalian hero Philoctetes with two of the arrows of Heracles, which had been dipped in the poisonous blood of the Hydra.note to war In Greek mythology, the hero Protesilaus was the first Greek to be killed at Troy, as soon as the army landed. After his death, according to Hyginus (Fables 104), his grieving wife Laodamia made a bronze image of him and devoted herself to it, and when her father Acastus tried to end her misery by burning the image on a pyre, she killed herself by jumping into the fire. The tomb of Protesilaus at Elaeus, on the Thracian Chersonesus (the modern Gallipoli peninsula), was the site of a famous devotional cult and site of pilgrimage in antiquity.gloss coast Regions, places or countries.gloss Nectarean Sweet as nectar.about at Dunmow The legendary infatuation of King John of England (1167–1216) for Matilda Fitzwalter culminated in her taking refuge in Dunmow Priory, where the king had her poisoned with a poached egg. The story was a popular subject in English poetry and drama in the late Renaissance.source so did Lucian’s Mercury wish In Lucian’s Dialogues of the Gods (17.1–2), Hermes (Mercury) says that he is jealous of Hephaestus (Vulcan), who married Aphrodite as well as Charis (or Aglaea, the youngest of the Graces), but admits that he has himself had intercourse with the former goddess.note that famous buckler of Argos The particular explanation given by Erasmus in his Adagia of the proverb, ‘He’s boasting as if he’d carried off an Argive shield’, refers to the holy shield possessed by the city of Argos, which could only be moved with great difficulty.about Spinola Don Mateo Serrano (c. 1550–1616) was governor of Sluis in the Low Countries, which was successfully besieged by Dutch and English troops in 1604. The Genoese aristocrat Ambrogio Spinola (1569–1630) was commander-in-chief of the Spanish army in Flanders.about The nine worthies In medieval and Renaissance chivalry, the nine figures of exemplary virtue drawn from myth, history and Scripture: Hector, Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, Joshua, David, Judas Maccabeus, King Arthur, Charlemagne and the Frankish knight Godfrey of Bouillon (1060–1100) – the last of these meriting inclusion on account of his reputation as the leader of the First Crusade, which captured Jerusalem.about Oliver and Roland Both ‘Paladins’ of the court of Charlemagne.gloss proof Impenetrable, invulnerable.note never make an end In Greek mythological interpretations of astronomy, the constellation of Canis Major (the ‘Greater Dog’) was commonly represented as being in perpetual pursuit of the Hare, the constellation Lepus. ‘Fatal’ here means ‘condemned by fate’ or ‘doomed’.about multitude of Moors This reference, from Baldassare Castiglione’s Libro del Cortegiano (1528), is to the conquest of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, by the joint forces of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile in the Granada War (1482–91).about Sir Walter Mauny Mauny (c. 1310–72) was a soldier and commander acclaimed for his gallantry and disregard of his own safety in Edward III’s campaigns in Scotland and France.gloss a proper man of person Physically attractive man.note smock The lewd response of Herleva (also known as ‘Arlotte’ as well as ‘Arlette’, and probably a tanner’s daughter) to the overtures of Robert, which led to the birth of William the Conqueror, was reputed to have been the origin of the English word ‘harlot’. In note ‘e’, ‘smock’ means ‘undergarment’, or ‘chemise’.note a Burgomaster’s daughter A ‘Burgomaster’ – an anachronistic term when used in an ancient context – was technically the chief magistrate of a Dutch or Flemish town. More loosely, it denoted a similar functionary in another foreign country.gloss complements A quality or accomplishment which ‘completes’ a gentleman.gloss Idiot Unskilled or untrained people.about Grobians A coarse, crude person (in Renaissance satire, ‘St Grobian’ was the fictional patron saint of the vulgarly ill-mannered).note nice, and too curious Both ‘nice’ and ‘curious’ here mean ‘fastidious’, or ‘exceedingly careful and precise’ – qualities often derogatorily attributed to contemporary puritans, who are also the ‘schismatics’ being accused here of destroying the unity of the English Church.gloss terse Refined, cultured.gloss smugs up Smartens.gloss band Collars or ruffs.gloss twires Twirls.gloss tire-woman Lady’s maid.gloss artificial impostures Illusory ornaments.source people first Julia Avita Mamaea (d. 235 CE) was actually the mother of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander. Herodian observes that during the festival of the sun-god Elagabalus, the emperor of the same name – whose mother Julia Soaemias Bassiana (d. 222) was Mamaea’s sister – used to parade around in ‘disgusting make-up’ (History of the Empire 5.7).note in Print Perfectly, precisely, neatly.about Philologia In this reference to the late-antique Carthaginian encyclopaedist Martianus Capella, ‘Mercury’ and ‘Philologia’ represent eloquence and learning respectively.about Suadela The Roman goddess of Persuasion.gloss distilling Trickling down, dripping.source Callistratus by the help of Daedalus … a-dancing Callistratus, in his account of the statue of Eros (Cupid) by the celebrated fourth-century BCE Athenian sculptor Praxiteles (Descriptions 3.12–15), says that its features made him believe that the mythical craftsman Daedalus, famous for his lifelike sculptures, had fashioned a troupe of dancers that really had movement and sensation (itself an allusion to the dance-floor Daedalus made for Ariadne in Crete: Iliad 18.590–93); ‘many’ here means ‘company’ or ‘retinue’.about the Hours The classical Horae, goddesses of the seasons.about Amphitrite In classical mythology, a sea-goddess and ruler of aquatic creatures, and the mother of the sea-nymphs known as the Nereids.about Hymenaeus The ancient name for a wedding song.gloss strawing Scattering.note wench asleep The sculpture, which is included in a list of sculptures from Roman tombs by Heinrich Kornmann in De miraculis mortuorum (1610), has not been identified, but it was presumably once located in the gardens of the Palazzo San Marco (now the Palazzo Venezia).about View of Fr. Note ‘f’ refers to The View of France (1604) by the English courtier Sir Robert Dallington.gloss mum Perform as a mummer, act in a mime.about Comus The classical god of festivity.about Hymen In classical mythology Hymen was a god of marriage ceremonies.note public Professor That is, a university professor, employed by the whole institution rather than a constituent college or a subsidiary body. In the course of his life, the philosopher Agostino Nifo (Niphus, c. 1469–c. 1546) had taught at Padua, Pisa, Naples and Salerno.note virginal Jacks The blocks of wood holding the quills that plucked the strings of a virginal, moving up and down as the instrument was played.about Trenchmore A boisterous English country dance.gloss prinkum-prankum Another name for the cushion-dance: see above, .gloss entreated Treat, deal with.source Lais of Corinth According to Aulus Gellius (1.8), Lais – on whom, see above, – charged 10,000 drachmas, or 10,000 denarii (one unit of each roughly corresponding to the average wage of a day-labourer). The figure of a hundred sesterces, which has evidently resulted from a mistranslation of the Latin terminology, undersells her services dramatically.see as Mundus to Paulina See above, .gloss likely Similarly.gloss Colewiz Chemnitz.about Herebertus Archbishop of Cologne Heribert of Cologne (970–1021).about Crommyomantia The name or initials inscribed on the first onion to sprout were taken to indicate the girl’s first suitor. fasting on St.about Anne’s Eve This should be the Eve of St Agnes, the patron saint of young girls and chastity, which is 20 January. Fasting on this occasion was said to induce a dream of the future husband.note Alphitomantia … by beans in a Cake Alphitomancy, divination using barley meal or barley cakes, and the similar practice of crithomancy, which used baked barley cakes. Both involved the interpretation of patterns found in the flour, or in the smoke produced when they were burned.gloss exornations Decorations, adornments.about Fescennines Verses or songs, traditionally sung at weddings and frequently obscene.source heard of According to Hyginus (Fables 273), the celebrations put on by the Libyan king Danaus for the wedding of his fifty daughters (the ‘Danaids’) included singing contests and the hymenaeus (‘wedding song’). The rest of the myth, in which under their father’s instructions they decapitate all but one of the bridegrooms on the wedding night, is not mentioned.note ’Tis true, Vulcan … dearly loved. A version of the classical myth of the necklace made by Vulcan for the goddess Harmonia (the daughter of Mars and Venus, not Hermione), which he had cursed in revenge for his cuckolding – see above, n. 10 (3.1.1). The account given by Parthenius of Nicaea (Sufferings in Love 25), from the Hellenistic historian Phylarchus, refers to the necklace’s passage, through the hands of the sons of the mythical Arcadian king Phegeus, down to the fourth century BCE and to the Phocian general Phayllus and the wife of Ariston, a leader of the Oetaean tribe in central Greece. Calamity eventually strikes her son goes mad and burns their house down, killing Ariston’s mother and destroying their possessions. On ‘ouche’, see above, .about Urania References to the Italian Renaissance poet Matteo Maria Boiardo (c. 1441–94), author of Orlando innamorato (1483), and two English writers, Sir Philip Sidney (1554–86) and Lady Mary Wroth (c. 1587–c. 1653), the latter being the author of the prose romance Urania (1621).gloss porteous Portable breviary, manual.about Astrophel’s Stella In Astrophil and Stella, the sonnet sequence written by Sir Philip Sidney in the 1580s. Roses, Violets, Lilies … etc.: The list of terms is taken from the criticisms given by the Italian humanist scholar and physician Julius Caesar Scaliger, in his Poetices libri septem (1561), of the verbal repetitiveness of Giovanni Pontano’s Tumuli (1505), a collection of poems addressed to dead friends and relatives. ‘Costus’ is the root of a variety of thistle (Saussurea costus), native to northern India; the oil from its root was used in medicine as well as perfumery.gloss hog rubbers Yokel, country bumpkin.about Menalcas and Corydon Generic names for shepherds in pastoral poetry.gloss accurate Carefully made.note Wakes, Whitsun ales The ‘Declaration of Sports’, issued by James I in 1617 and 1618, and again by Charles I in 1633, permitted various sports and recreations on Sundays and other holy days, including ‘May games’, ‘Whitsun ales’ (parish celebrations at Whitsuntide involving ale-drinking and other entertainments) and, in 1633, ‘wakes’. It was published in order to resolve a dispute that had arisen in Lancashire between puritans and gentry.gloss roundelays Folk dances in which the dancers form a circle.about lovers’ knots In note ‘f’, a ‘true-love knot’ was an ornamental knot (a double-looped bow or two intertwined loops) symbolizing true love.note bonny Broom The title of a song included in John Playford’s English Dancing Master (1651), but also a line from the traditional love ballad ‘The Broom of Cowdenknows’.note Bess a Bell she doth excel A folk song sometimes entitled ‘Bessy Bell she doth excel’.gloss indite Express or dictate words for a literary composition.source his diet See above, . ‘Myunte’ here refers to the small Ionian port of Myus, reportedly granted to the exiled Athenian politician and general Themistocles for its abundance of fish (Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 11.57.7).source her hood According to Cicero (Against Verres 2.33.76), the wives of Persian and Syrian kings were provided with specific adornments by different towns in their territories.gloss to buy her pins That is, as ‘pin money’ – an allowance for clothing and personal expenses.about Antinoe More usually Antinopolis, now Sheikh Ibada, on the east bank of the Nile.about Constellations … Antinous The constellation named by Hadrian after Antinous – on whom, see above, – is now obsolete in astronomy, and is regarded as part of Aquila.note set out his Hephaestion to all eternity That is, adorn him for his funeral. On Hephaestion, see above, .gloss sectator Follower, disciple.note ut occluso stillat ab igne liquor The Latin quotation is found in several Renaissance emblematic representations of love, which depict Cupid working at his still (and using fire to produce tears).note hanc An aside delivered to the slave Parmeno by the young Athenian Phaedria, at the entrance of his beloved prostitute Thais, in Terence’s Eunuch (83–4).note huc ades O Thelayra The first line of a love song presented in Girolamo Fracastoro’s Naugerius sive de poetica dialogus (1549).source first give an hundred … more, &c. A quotation from The Forest (6.8–13) by Ben Jonson, which appeared in the first folio edition of his works (1616). The reference in note ‘a’ to him as ‘our arch-Poet’ (poet-laureate) is slightly misleading, as he was never formally given this title, but he had been granted a royal pension in February 1616.source Sphinx’s wings According to Plutarch, in a fragment (136) quoting the Oedipus of Euripides, the Theban Sphinx – see above, – had multicoloured wings.source Agnae In this quotation from Horace (Satires 1.3.39–40), ‘Balbinus’ may refer to one of the victims of the proscriptions issued in 43 BCE after the assassination of Julius Caesar. ‘Hagna’ has not been identified, but this was a common name among Roman freedwomen.about Doris The mother of Galatea and the other Nereids. Burton is referring to the first of Lucian’s Dialogues of the Sea-Gods.source venit In this line from Ovid’s Fasti (2.332), Faunus is the Roman god of the outdoors, equivalent to the Greek Pan. Here, the goat-like deity is on his way to rape the Lydian queen Omphale, but inadvertently molests Hercules (Heracles) instead.about Squire of Dames A comic character in Spenser’s Faerie Queene. · note Knight of the Sun Late medieval French and Spanish chivalric romances, popular among the gentry and nobility in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and parodied in Don Quixote. · about Sir Bevis of Southampton Bevis of Hampton (or ‘Sir Bevois’), an English hero found in many medieval romances. · note that renowned peer, Orlando … undertake Orlando (the Italian form of Roland) was one of the ‘Paladins’, or ‘Twelve Peers’ – warriors who served Charlemagne and were celebrated in The Song of Roland as paragons of Christian virtue.gloss pour Make great effort, give their all. · gloss stour Armed contest. · gloss rivelled Shrivelled, wrinkled.note busk point The lace and tag securing a corset’s busk (the supporting frame attached to its front section).note bedfellows In Plautus’ Braggart Soldier (65), the parasite Artotrogus flatters the pompous Pyrgopolynices by reporting that a woman said this about him. · source as she said of Cyrus … but a night In the anecdote related in Xenophon’s Cyropaedia (5.2.28), these words were actually said about an anonymous young man by a concubine of Abradatas, the (fictitious) king of Susa, who promptly had him castrated.note a Novizza or Venetian Bride In Renaissance Venice, a future bride was called a ‘Novizza’.note lovelock Or just ‘lock’ – a lock of hair worn longer than the rest, hanging forward over one shoulder, as was fashionable among male courtiers. · about Ganymede Catamites or young male prostitutes – senses which derive from the homoerotic aspect of the mythological tale related above, . · note as Heinsius writ to Primerius Daniel Heinsius’ letter of July 1607 to his fellow poet and scholar Jacob Primerius has the title ‘Qualis viro literato ducenda sit uxor? &, an ducenda?’ (‘What kind of wife should be taken by a learned man? And should he take one?’) · gloss prune Preening its feathers. · gloss pique-devant With a short beard trimmed to a point. · about Julian the Apostate … Misopogon In his satirical Misopogon (‘Beard-hater’), written in 363 as a reply to Christian critics in Antioch, Julian begins by quoting their ridicule of his beard and contrasting his shaggy, philosophical appearance with that of the smooth-skinned, sophisticated citizens of the city – before turning the abuse on to them. · note to follow mine author Burton has returned to Heinsius.about Golden Fleece See above, . The Order of the Golden Fleece is a Catholic chivalric order founded by Philip the Good, duke of Burgundy, in 1430.note under the plane tree An allusion to Plato’s Phaedrus, which is set under a plane tree outside the walls of Athens, on the banks of the River Ilissus.
